newsitem.title: UK: Albright urges NATO enlargement by 1999.
newsitem.headline: Albright urges NATO enlargement by 1999.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday the Clinton administration had "no higher priority" than to enlarge NATO by 1999 and Russia need have nothing to fear.
On the eve of her first trip abroad in her new post, Albright said that just the prospect of NATO enlargement had given Central and Eastern Europe greater stability than at any time this century.

"At the NATO summit this July in Madrid, allied leaders will reform NATO's internal structures and invite several nations to become members by 1999," she said in article in Britain's Economist magazine.
"President Clinton and I have no higher priority than to work with our allies, and with our people and Congress, to build this new NATO."

Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are front runners to join the 16-nation North Atlantic alliance, with Romania and Slovenia close behind. NATO is trying to win round a deeply hostile Russia to its expansion plans, with the promise of a strengthened relationship.
Enlargement must begin with the strongest candidates, Albright said, but the first new members would not be the last.

Albright, appointed Secretary of State by Clinton after his re-election last November, will at the weekend begin an 11-day tour of Europe and Asia, which includes meetings with Russian leaders in Moscow.

With NATO's future perhaps the most controversial foreign policy question of the post-Cold War era, Albright said the alliance had made a strong case for enlargement, while opponents were trapped in "old thinking".
"It is high time that critics came forward with a rationale that might possibly support a policy of fossilized immobility in the face of Europe's sweeping changes," she said.

"Now that democracy's frontier has moved to Europe's farthest reaches, what logic would dictate that we freeze NATO's eastern edges where they presently lie, along the line where the Red Army stopped in the spring of 1945?"
Critics were mistaking NATO's real value when they said none of its prospective members faced an immediate military threat.
"The alliance is not a wild west posse that we trot out only when danger appears," Albright said. "NATO does not need an enemy. It has enduring purposes."

Albright dismissed suggestions that NATO enlargement would somehow redivide post-Cold War Europe, saying NATO had taken steps "to ensure that the erasure of old lines of division does not leave new ones on the map".
On Moscow's opposition to an enlarged NATO, Albright said "the NATO Russia claims to oppose bears little resemblance to the alliance we are actually building".

She said: "It is a mistake to think that the fate of Russian democracy is somehow at stake in the enlargement debate...The Russian people know that their future will be written in Moscow, in Perm, in Irkutsk, and certainly not in Brussels."
Albright said NATO wanted a charter that would set up a permanent NATO-Russia joint council, with Russia participating in NATO's Combined Joint Task Forces.
